notes.meaning: The Lord gave Ezekiel a new message to deliver. After speaking about the entire city of Tyre in the previous chapters, God now singled out its ruler.

The ruler of Tyre had grown proud and claimed that he was a god, sitting safely in an island fortress that no enemy could touch. God reminded him that he was only a mortal man, subject to weakness and death.

The prophet spoke with biting sarcasm, mockingly asking if the ruler thought he was wiser than Daniel. Daniel was already famous across the Babylonian empire for his God-given wisdom, but the king of Tyre proudly thought no secret was beyond his own mind.

The ruler had used his sharp business skills and sea trade to pile up enormous amounts of silver and gold. Having great wealth is not an evil by itself, but it deceived the king into becoming arrogant and self-reliant.

Because the king acted as if he had the heart and mind of a god, the Lord promised to bring ruthless foreign invaders against him. The Babylonian army would soon march against Tyre, stripping away all the treasures and honor that the king took pride in.

These invaders would drag the king down to the grave, giving him a violent death in the waters that once made him feel safe. His watery stronghold would not be a divine throne, but the place where his life ended.

The Lord asked whether the king would still boast of being a god while facing the soldier sent to kill him. Facing execution would instantly prove that he was completely helpless, just like any other mortal man.

The king was told he would die like an outsider who had no part in God's covenant, killed by foreign soldiers. For an ancient leader who prided himself on honor, dying an uncircumcised death meant dying in total shame and disgrace.

Ezekiel was told to sing a funeral song over the king of Tyre. The song began by describing the ruler as someone who seemed to have everything, picturing him as a pattern of complete beauty and wisdom before his terrible fall.

differ.view: The funeral song looks past the human king of Tyre to describe the unfallen glory of Satan, the spiritual power at work behind proud earthly rulers.

notes.meaning: The funeral song pictures the king as enjoying a paradise like the Garden of Eden, clothed with brilliant jewels. God gave him great royal honor and celebration from the day he came to power, yet he took credit for it all himself.

differ.view: The mention of Eden and jewels describes Satan in his original glory serving in God's presence before he rebelled.

notes.meaning: The poem compares the king to a protective cherub, an angel like those that guarded holy places. God placed him in a position of royal dignity and power, surrounded by flashing gems, so he was expected to protect and govern his people wisely.
The ruler began his reign with great success, wisdom, and honor. That blameless start ended when wickedness and selfish ambition took root inside his heart.

Tyre's vast international trade led to greed, dishonest dealing, and violent oppression. Because the king tolerated and took part in this wickedness, God removed him from his place of honor and cast him out in disgrace.

The king became conceited because of his wealth and glory, which warped his good judgment. As a result, the Lord threw him down to the ground, leaving him ruined in front of other kings as a warning against pride.

Dishonest trade and wicked actions ruined the sacred honors and royal places the king claimed to hold. The Lord brought about his destruction from within his own sins, reducing his greatness to ashes on the ground for everyone to see.

Neighboring nations that once admired Tyre's wealth and power were shocked by its sudden fall. The king's ruin was permanent and terrifying, proving that earthly empires cannot stand against God's judgment.

The Lord told Ezekiel to turn his attention northward to the Phoenician city of Sidon and speak a message of judgment against it. Sidon was an older sister city to Tyre and had long led the region into idolatry.

God declared that He was opposed to Sidon and would display His justice through her punishment. By judging the city for its wickedness, the Lord would prove to all people that He is holy and truly God.

Sidon would suffer severe disasters, including deadly disease and invading armies fighting in her streets. Through these terrible losses, the survivors would realize that the Lord alone has supreme authority.

Neighboring nations had hurt and mocked Israel like sharp briers and stinging thorns, drawing them into idol worship and rejoicing over their troubles. God promised to remove these hostile neighbors so His people would no longer be mistreated.

The Lord promised to bring the people of Israel back from the nations where they had been scattered and settle them safely in their own land. Once their enemies were judged, God's people would build homes, plant vineyards, and live in lasting peace, knowing that the Lord is their faithful God.

differ.view: This promise of complete safety and rebuilding looks beyond the return from Babylon to a future time when Christ reigns on earth.
The promise began in the return under Zerubbabel and reaches its true spiritual fulfillment in the church gathered under Christ.
